recall_prompt: Say how you would answer this — give the definition in set form, and say what your example would show.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: State the definition
steps.margin_note: First mark. The set-builder line A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A and b ∈ B} earns it. The word ordered must be there — a definition without it is incomplete.
lines: Let A and B be two non-empty sets.
The Cartesian product of A and B, written A × B, is the set of all ordered pairs
whose first entry is taken from A and whose second entry is taken from B.
A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A and b ∈ B}

recall.must_convey: That A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B.
accept: A cross B is the set of all ordered pairs a comma b with a in A and b in B
every element of A paired with every element of B
the set of ordered pairs first from A second from B
A lo prathi element ni B lo prathi element tho pair cheyyali
state it as a set of ordered pairs

steps.why: The word ordered is the whole of the definition: (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different elements of a Cartesian product, and that is what makes A × B different from B × A.
steps.memory_tip: The first entry always comes from the first set — that is why it is A × B and not B × A.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the word ordered, so the definition would treat (a, b) and (b, a) as the same.
Writing A × B = {a, b : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}, which is a set of elements rather than a set of pairs.

steps.label: Show it on an example
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Four pairs, each in round brackets. The examiner checks that every element of A has been paired with every element of B, and that the count matches n(A) · n(B).
lines: Pair each element of A with each element of B:

recall.must_convey: That a small example is worked out in full, giving all four ordered pairs.
accept: take A as one two and B as x y and write all four pairs
one with x one with y two with x two with y
the number of pairs is two times two which is four
prathi element ni prathi element tho kalipi four pairs rasta
list every pair with the first entry from A

steps.why: The example is only complete when every pairing is present, so the count n(A) · n(B) = 4 is written beside it as the check. Reversing the sets here would give B × A = {(x, 1), (x, 2), (y, 1), (y, 2)}, a different set.
steps.memory_tip: Take the first element of A with every element of B, then the second element of A with every element of B.
common_mistakes: Writing the pairs with curly brackets, which makes each pair a set and loses the order.
Writing only (1, x) and (2, y), one pair per element instead of all four.
Giving B × A instead of A × B.
